lines.t: Welcome back. Today we turn to a word that appears in almost every discussion of good government: transparency. What does it actually mean?
In simple terms, transparency means that the public can see how decisions are made, how money is spent, and who is responsible.
The idea is that officials behave better when they know people are watching.
Let me break the concept into three parts. The first is the right to request information.
Many countries now have freedom of information laws, which allow citizens to ask for official documents.
The earliest such law was passed in Sweden in the eighteenth century, though most others appeared after nineteen sixty.
The second part is proactive publication. Instead of waiting for requests, governments publish budgets, contracts and meeting records on their own initiative.
This saves citizens the trouble of asking, and it saves officials the trouble of answering.
The third part is participation. Transparency is more useful when people can attend public meetings, comment on draft laws and report concerns.
Let me give an example. Imagine a city that decides to publish every contract worth more than ten thousand dollars.
Within months, a local journalist notices that three different schools paid very different prices for identical desks.
Questions are asked, the supplier is changed, and the city saves money. Nobody needed to prove corruption; simply seeing the information was enough.
However, transparency has limits. Some information must stay confidential, such as personal medical records or details of national security.
The challenge is to decide where to draw the line, and the usual principle is that secrecy needs a clear reason, while openness needs none.
There is a second limitation. Publishing a huge number of documents is not the same as being open.
If the files are in a confusing format or buried on a website nobody can find, citizens learn nothing. Critics call this a data dump.
Real transparency means information that is easy to find, to read and to compare.
Finally, remember that transparency alone does not punish anyone. It must be connected to accountability, which means there are consequences when officials misuse their power.
Without that, people may see the problem clearly but feel unable to change it.
In our next session, we will look at the tools that connect transparency to accountability. Thank you.

lines.t: Good morning. Today's topic is how machines learn from data, a subject that sounds mysterious but rests on a few simple ideas.
Let us start with a comparison. In traditional programming, a person writes the rules. If an email contains the words free prize, mark it as spam.
The computer follows the rules exactly, but it only catches what the programmer thought of.
Machine learning reverses this.
Instead of writing rules, we give the computer thousands of examples, each labelled as spam or not spam, and a learning algorithm looks for patterns that separate the two groups.
The result is called a model.
This approach is known as supervised learning, because the examples come with correct answers, like a teacher marking homework.
It is the most common type used today, for tasks such as recognising faces or predicting house prices.
A crucial step is testing. Researchers usually keep about twenty percent of their data hidden during training.
After training, they show the model this unseen data and measure how often it is right.
If they tested on the same examples used for learning, the results would be misleadingly good.
That brings us to overfitting. An overfitted model has memorised the training examples, including their accidental details, instead of learning general patterns.
It is like a student who memorises last year's exam paper and then fails when the questions change.
The second type is unsupervised learning. Here there are no labels, and the algorithm simply searches for natural groups.
A shop might use it to discover that its customers fall into four distinct kinds of buyer, without anyone telling the computer what to look for.
The third type is reinforcement learning. The system tries actions and receives rewards or penalties, so it improves through trial and error.
This is how programs have learned to play complex board games, sometimes playing millions of games against themselves.
Now an important warning. A model learns whatever patterns are in its data, including unfair ones.
Suppose a company trains a hiring tool on the records of past employees, and most of those employees were men.
The tool may learn to prefer men, not because anyone intended it, but because the data reflected the past.
This is why data quality matters more than data quantity.
And it is why people who work in law and public policy need to understand these systems well enough to question them.
Next time, we will look at how to audit an algorithm. Thank you.

lines.t: Hello everyone. Today we are going to ask why some languages die, and whether anything can be done about it.
There are roughly seven thousand languages in the world today.
Linguists estimate that around forty percent are endangered, and many experts think about half may disappear by the end of this century.
First, what does it mean for a language to die? It does not happen with a sudden disaster.
A language is usually considered dead when its last fluent speaker passes away.
But the real turning point comes much earlier, when parents stop passing the language on to their children.
Why do parents make that choice? The most common reason is economic.
If good jobs and university courses require a dominant language, families naturally want their children to master it.
They are not rejecting their heritage; they are trying to give their children opportunities.
Migration is a second factor. When young people move from villages to big cities, they live and work among speakers of other languages.
Their own language is heard only at home, and then less and less.
Schools and media play a role as well.
If lessons, television and the internet are all in one national language, a small language has no place in modern life.
Sometimes there is also social pressure, so that speakers feel embarrassed to use their language in public.
Interestingly, the number of speakers is not the only measure of health. A language with a million speakers can be in danger if no children are learning it.
A language with only a few thousand speakers can survive if the community uses it daily.
Why should we care?
Each language holds a unique store of knowledge, for example names for local plants, traditional methods of navigation or farming, and stories that exist nowhere else.
When the language disappears, much of that knowledge goes with it.
There are encouraging examples. In Wales, the Welsh language has been supported through schools and television, and the number of young speakers has risen.
In New Zealand, communities created preschools where small children learn Maori entirely through the language.
Modern technology helps too, since speakers can record words and make learning apps cheaply.
The lesson is that revival is possible, but it needs children, and it needs the community to want it. Thank you.

lines.t: Good morning. Today we are going to look at the economics of water, which raises a puzzle that economists have discussed for hundreds of years.
The puzzle is this. Water is essential for life, yet in most places it is very cheap. Diamonds are not essential, yet they are extremely expensive. Why?
The traditional answer is that price depends not on how useful something is overall, but on how scarce it is at the moment of buying.
Where water is plentiful, the next litre has little value.
But water is becoming scarce. About ninety-seven percent of the planet's water is salty, and most of the fresh water is frozen or underground.
The share that is easy to reach is tiny.
Agriculture is the biggest user. Around seventy percent of the fresh water taken from rivers and wells worldwide goes to irrigation.
This means that small improvements in farming can save more water than large changes in households.
One problem is that farmers and households often pay prices that are far below the true cost of delivering water.
Governments keep prices low for good reasons, to protect poorer people, but the effect is waste, because nobody has a reason to save.
One solution is tiered pricing. The first portion of water, enough for drinking, cooking and washing, is cheap. Further portions cost more per litre.
In this way, essential use is protected while heavy use is discouraged.
A second issue is leakage. In some cities, as much as a third of the treated water is lost through broken pipes before it reaches a tap.
Repairing them is often cheaper than finding new sources, but repairs are invisible and politicians prefer to cut ribbons on new dams.
Third, there is the idea of virtual water, the water used to produce goods.
Producing one kilogram of beef takes thousands of litres, whereas a kilogram of wheat takes far fewer. When a dry country imports food, it is effectively importing water.
Finally, fairness. In many places, poor households without a connection buy water from vendors and pay several times more per litre than wealthy neighbours who have pipes.
Solving this requires investment in networks, not simply lower prices.
To conclude, water is an economic problem as well as an environmental one. Thank you.

title: How scientists test a new medicine

lines.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to explain how scientists test a new medicine before it reaches the pharmacy, a process that often takes ten years or more.
It begins in the laboratory. Researchers test a promising substance on cells and then on animals, to see whether it seems to work and whether it is toxic.
Most substances fail at this early stage, and only a few move forward.
The next step is human testing, which is divided into phases. In phase one, a small group of volunteers, usually between twenty and one hundred, receive the medicine.
The main question is safety. Researchers find the highest dose that people can tolerate without serious side effects.
In phase two, the medicine is given to a few hundred patients who actually have the illness.
Now the question is whether it works, and what dose is best.
Phase three is the largest and most expensive. Thousands of patients take part, often in many countries.
The new medicine is compared either with the best existing treatment or with a placebo, which is a harmless pill with no active ingredient.
Why use a placebo? Because simply believing you are being treated can make you feel better.
To separate that effect from the medicine itself, patients are assigned to groups at random, by a computer, so that the groups are similar.
In the best trials, the design is double-blind. This means neither the patients nor the doctors know who is receiving the real medicine until the trial is finished.
Otherwise, doctors might unconsciously treat or judge the groups differently.
When phase three is complete, the company sends all the results to a regulatory agency.
Independent experts examine the data, and if the benefits clearly outweigh the risks, the medicine is approved.
But testing does not stop there.
In phase four, doctors continue to monitor patients after approval, because rare side effects may appear only when hundreds of thousands of people use the medicine.
One more point, which is important for public trust.
In many countries, companies must register a trial before it begins and must report the results, even if the medicine failed.
Without this rule, disappointing results could simply be hidden, and doctors would see only the success stories.
To summarise, good testing needs several phases, random groups, blind design and honest reporting. Thank you.
